summary: This standards-track document describes using the Network Service Header with Service Function Chaining where there is no payload, only metadata. It does this by defining a new Next Protocol value of None. It illustrates functions that this can support.

plainLanguage.summary: Sometimes a mail envelope carries only a note on the outside and nothing inside. This lets the service chain header do exactly that.

questions: what is the nsh none next protocol
what is nsh next protocol none
what is a service function path
why rate limit nsh metadata packets
subtitle: A new Next Protocol value lets a service-chain packet carry only metadata and no user data.

tldr.problem: Nodes on a Service Function Path sometimes need to share metadata, for example for monitoring or coordination, but the NSH normally travels with a data packet.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines Next Protocol value 0x00, "None", meaning no payload follows the NSH. The NSH and its metadata still count, and nodes process them as usual.
tldr.outcome: Metadata can be sent without traffic flowing. The extra packets risk congestion, so implementations SHOULD rate limit them.

facts.label: Default rate limit
facts.value: One per ten data packets per flow

today: RFC 8393 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the NSH defined in RFC 8300.

sections.title: Why Send Metadata Alone
sections.content:
In the Service Function Chaining (SFC) architecture (RFC 7665), packets follow a Service Function Path (SFP) through Service Functions. Each packet carries a Network Service Header (NSH, RFC 8300) with a Service Path Identifier (SPI) and a Service Index (SI).

The classifier or any SFC-aware service function instance may want to share information about the path, a flow or a packet. It does this with metadata in the NSH. This RFC lets metadata travel without payload data. That supports diagnosis and monitoring of paths and coordination between instances, and it works even when no traffic is flowing. When traffic is flowing, it avoids inserting large amounts of metadata into data packets, which can be costly in some hardware.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally a note rides along stuck to a parcel. Here you can send the note by itself, even when there are no parcels going by.

sections.title: Next Protocol None
sections.content:
The NSH has a Next Protocol field that says what kind of payload follows. This RFC defines the value 0x00, meaning "None": no user or payload data follows the NSH.

The rest of the NSH keeps its meaning, and metadata may still be present. A packet with "None" is not meant to carry no metadata, so a node SHOULD NOT create one with Metadata Type 0x2 and an NSH Length of 0x2.
sections.plainLanguage: A label on the parcel says what is inside. The new label says "nothing", but the note on the outside still counts.

sections.title: Processing Rules
sections.content:
A metadata-only packet may be inserted at the head of an SFP, or generated by an instance after processing a normal packet. The SPI and SI can be inherited from the original packet or set through the control plane, the management plane, or metadata in the data packet. The RFC does not specify what triggers such packets.

A node sending one MUST create a packet with an NSH and the metadata, MUST set Next Protocol to 0x00, SHOULD leave no bytes after the NSH, and MUST send it as for any NSH packet. A transit node MUST NOT parse beyond the end of the NSH but SHOULD process the NSH and metadata as normal. An egress node MUST NOT forward such a packet, even if bytes follow the NSH. Administrators who do not want the feature SHOULD tell nodes not to create these packets and to discard them.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender writes the note and marks the parcel as empty. Helpers along the way read the note but never open the parcel. At the end of the road, nobody delivers it.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
Nodes that do not know a Next Protocol value silently drop the packet unless configured to forward it (Section 2.2 of RFC 8300). Legacy nodes that do not know "None" behave differently by role.

  • SFFs can be configured to forward the packets.
  • SFC proxies will drop them.
  • SFIs and classifiers will most likely drop them.
sections.plainLanguage: Older helpers do not know the new "empty" label. Some will pass it on, but most will throw it away.

sections.title: Use Cases
sections.content:
The RFC illustrates uses without claiming a complete list.

  • Per-SFP metadata applies to a path and its data packets, and can be installed at points of consumption instead of being sent with every packet.
  • Per-flow metadata applies to a subset such as a 5-tuple. With "None" there is no payload to inspect, so the flow identity is carried in the metadata itself.
  • Coordination between two instances needs an SFP through both, the right SPI and the right SI. A dedicated SFP may be used just for this.
  • OAM can be sent when no other traffic flows, at predictable intervals, and without rewriting payload buffers.
  • Control and management plane messages, with SFPs serving as a Data Control Network or Management Control Network.

Per-packet metadata is not applicable, because with no payload there is no packet to attach it to.
sections.plainLanguage: You can use an empty parcel to pass notes between helpers, to check the road is working, or to send instructions. You cannot use it for a note about one particular parcel, because there is none.

sections.title: Congestion and Rate Limits
sections.content:
Extra packets can flood the network. For instance, per-packet use might double the packet count, and very frequent aliveness tests could add many messages. The underlay does not distinguish these packets from data packets.

All implementations SHOULD rate limit generation of such packets, configurably per SFP and per application, and SHOULD count packets they cannot send. They SHOULD also apply incoming rate limits and count drops. Alerts MAY be raised but SHOULD themselves be rate limited. The suggested default is no more than one "None" packet per ten data packets on any flow, in a unit of time equal to the end-to-end delivery time.
sections.plainLanguage: If everyone sends empty parcels all the time, the road jams. So each sender gets a small allowance.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Metadata-only packets provide a covert channel, though this differs from normal NSH metadata only in that no data flow is needed. Metadata may be sensitive or control the behavior of instances, so it needs protection, for example encrypted transport, encrypted metadata and sender authentication.

The mechanism could be used to inject false metadata. Measures SHOULD ensure authorization of sources, tunneling of such packets into the network SHOULD be prevented, and the amount of such packets SHOULD be rate limited at each point on the path.
sections.plainLanguage: A note with no parcel could be forged. So only trusted senders may put notes on the road, and there is a limit on how many.
